questions.text: Which statement best captures the economic problem of scarcity?

options.a: Every good has a positive money price.
options.b: Resources are limited relative to the wants they could be used to satisfy.
options.c: People are unable to compare alternative uses of resources.
options.d: Firms always face shortages of labor.

questions.text: Microeconomics is primarily concerned with

options.a: the determination of a country’s long-run growth rate only.
options.b: the accounting rules used to construct the balance of payments.
options.c: the measurement of national income and aggregate unemployment only.
options.d: the behavior and choices of individual economic decision makers such as consumers and firms.

questions.text: Which of the following can be a microeconomic question?

options.a: What determines the national unemployment rate over the business cycle.
options.b: How a tax on a particular good changes the choices of consumers and firms in that market.
options.c: How aggregate output is measured in national accounts.
options.d: How the overall price level changes across the entire economy.

questions.text: An economic model is best described as

options.a: a simplified formal description of an economic problem built on explicit assumptions.
options.b: a forecast that is valid only if every variable is endogenous.
options.c: a complete description of reality with no simplifying assumptions.
options.d: a historical narrative that contains no variables.

questions.text: In an economic model, an exogenous variable is a variable whose value is

options.a: chosen by the consumer in the objective function.
options.b: taken as given by the model.
options.c: determined by solving the model.
options.d: always equal to zero in equilibrium.

questions.text: In an economic model, an endogenous variable is a variable whose value is

options.a: measured outside the model but not explained by it.
options.b: fixed by assumption and never allowed to change.
options.c: necessarily controlled by the government.
options.d: determined within the model.

questions.text: Constrained optimization refers to

options.a: maximizing every possible objective at the same time.
options.b: comparing two equilibria after an exogenous change.
options.c: choosing the best feasible alternative while respecting restrictions on the choice.
options.d: setting prices so that quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.

questions.text: In a constrained optimization problem, the objective function describes

options.a: the exogenous variables that must remain constant forever.
options.b: the restrictions that define the feasible set.
options.c: the price adjustment rule that clears a market.
options.d: the relationship the decision maker seeks to maximize or minimize.

questions.text: In a constrained optimization problem, a constraint is

options.a: the marginal benefit of the last unit chosen.
options.b: the value of the objective at the optimum.
options.c: a variable determined only after equilibrium is reached.
options.d: a restriction or limit imposed on the decision maker’s choices.

questions.text: The standard rational-choice assumption used in the slides is that a decision maker

options.a: tries to choose the best alternative available to them.
options.b: never changes behavior when incentives change.
options.c: always chooses the cheapest alternative regardless of preferences.
options.d: always has perfect information about every future event.

questions.text: Why can a brewery optimally split an advertising budget between TV and radio even if TV generates more total sales than radio at every equal spending level?

options.a: Radio advertising must have a larger total effect at every spending level.
options.b: Optimal allocation depends on marginal effects, not simply on total effects at equal spending levels.
options.c: Rational firms ignore diminishing marginal effects when allocating a fixed budget.
options.d: The budget constraint does not apply to advertising decisions.

questions.text: The term “marginal” in microeconomics refers to

options.a: the change in a dependent variable caused by a small additional unit of an independent variable.
options.b: a change in an exogenous variable that leaves all endogenous variables fixed.
options.c: the total level of a variable before any choice is made.
options.d: the average value of all feasible alternatives.

questions.text: Diminishing marginal impact of advertising means that

options.a: the first euro spent has no effect on sales.
options.b: the marginal impact is constant at every level of spending.
options.c: total sales must eventually become negative.
options.d: additional spending generates smaller and smaller increments in sales as spending rises.

questions.text: An equilibrium is a state that

options.a: must involve zero profits for every firm in every market.
options.b: can exist only when government fixes the market price.
options.c: will persist as long as relevant exogenous factors remain unchanged.
options.d: requires every individual to consume identical bundles.

questions.text: The equilibrium principle used for the apartment market says that prices adjust until

options.a: quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
options.b: all apartments have identical quality.
options.c: every renter has the same reservation price.
options.d: the supply curve becomes horizontal.

questions.text: A renter’s reservation price is

options.a: the rent of the renter’s outside option by definition.
options.b: the lowest rent a landlord is legally allowed to charge.
options.c: the highest rent the renter is willing to pay for an apartment.
options.d: the market-clearing rent after all trades occur.

questions.text: All else equal, when the rental price of city-center apartments falls, the quantity demanded tends to

options.a: increase because more potential renters have reservation prices above the rent.
options.b: remain unchanged because reservation prices adjust one-for-one with rent.
options.c: become zero unless the price equals the equilibrium price.
options.d: decrease because supply is fixed in the short run.

questions.text: In the short-run apartment-market example, the supply curve is vertical because

options.a: the number of available apartments is fixed in the short run.
options.b: demand is perfectly elastic.
options.c: the equilibrium price is fixed by assumption.
options.d: landlords have identical reservation prices.

questions.text: If the apartment rent is below the equilibrium rent, then

options.a: quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded and the rent tends to rise.
options.b: quantity demanded is below quantity supplied and the rent tends to fall.
options.c: quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied and the rent tends to rise.
options.d: quantity demanded equals quantity supplied automatically.

questions.text: If the apartment rent is above the equilibrium rent, then

options.a: quantity demanded and quantity supplied both become zero.
options.b: quantity demanded is below quantity supplied and the rent tends to fall.
options.c: quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied and the rent tends to rise.
options.d: the market must remain permanently out of equilibrium.

questions.text: In the simple apartment-market model, an efficient market allocation assigns apartments to

options.a: renters selected randomly, regardless of willingness to pay.
options.b: only those whose reservation price equals zero.
options.c: the people with the lowest reservation prices.
options.d: the people with the greatest willingness to pay.

questions.text: Comparative statics is the method of

options.a: measuring only changes in accounting identities.
options.b: tracing the exact time path by which a market moves between equilibria.
options.c: comparing two static equilibria before and after a change in an exogenous variable.
options.d: maximizing a utility function without any constraints.

questions.text: Comparative statics generally does NOT tell us

options.a: how the equilibrium may differ after an exogenous change.
options.b: which variables are endogenous in a specified model.
options.c: the dynamic path the market follows from the old equilibrium to the new equilibrium.
options.d: whether a supply or demand shift changes equilibrium outcomes.

questions.text: If new city-center apartments are constructed, the standard comparative-statics prediction is

options.a: a lower equilibrium rent with no change in equilibrium quantity.
options.b: an ambiguous quantity effect and a necessarily higher rent.
options.c: a lower equilibrium rent and a higher equilibrium quantity of rented apartments.
options.d: a higher equilibrium rent and a lower equilibrium quantity.

questions.text: Suppose some rental apartments are converted into owner-occupied condominiums, reducing both rental supply and rental demand. Which outcome is unambiguous in the slides?

options.a: The equilibrium rent must fall.
options.b: The equilibrium quantity of rental apartments falls.
options.c: The equilibrium rent must rise.
options.d: The equilibrium quantity of rental apartments rises.

questions.text: When both rental supply and rental demand decrease, the effect on the equilibrium rent can be ambiguous because

options.a: the equilibrium principle no longer applies.
options.b: the supply shift tends to raise rent while the demand shift tends to lower rent.
options.c: both shifts necessarily raise rent by the same amount.
options.d: prices do not respond to simultaneous supply and demand shifts.

questions.text: Which statement correctly distinguishes constrained optimization from equilibrium analysis?

options.a: Constrained optimization studies the best feasible choice of a decision maker, whereas equilibrium analysis studies mutual consistency of choices in a system such as a market.
options.b: Constrained optimization concerns only firms, while equilibrium analysis concerns only consumers.
options.c: Constrained optimization determines exogenous variables, while equilibrium analysis fixes all endogenous variables by assumption.
options.d: They are the same analytical tool with different names.

questions.text: Refer to the accompanying figure. What does the point where the demand curve intersects the vertical supply curve represent?

options.a: A rent below equilibrium at which there is excess supply.
options.b: The maximum reservation price in the market regardless of supply.
options.c: A rent above equilibrium at which there is excess demand.
options.d: The market-clearing rent p* at which the fixed apartment supply equals quantity demanded.

questions.text: If an exogenous variable changes in a model, the purpose of comparative statics is to ask

options.a: which exogenous variable the model should redefine as endogenous after the change.
options.b: how the model’s endogenous equilibrium outcomes change as a result.
options.c: whether the original assumptions can be discarded entirely.
options.d: how to keep every endogenous variable fixed despite the change.

questions.text: Why are assumptions useful in economic models?

options.a: They simplify reality so that important mechanisms and relationships can be analyzed clearly.
options.b: They guarantee that a model will predict every real-world observation exactly.
options.c: They ensure that all economic decisions are unconstrained.
options.d: They eliminate the need to distinguish exogenous from endogenous variables.
